sections.h2: What is the Georgia eviction process called, and where does it run?
sections.html:
Georgia calls it a dispossessory proceeding, and the landlord starts it by filing a sworn affidavit, sometimes called the eviction warrant, asking the court to return the property and award unpaid rent. Georgia Courts explains that without that filing and a court order a landlord has no legal way to remove a tenant.

Most of these cases are filed in magistrate court because that court can be easier to navigate and may move faster. The handbook notes they can also go to state or superior court, or to some municipal courts, and a few magistrate courts take filings online. The case belongs in the county where the rental house sits.

sections.h2: What does the landlord's affidavit have to say?
sections.html:
It must be made under oath and carry five items, according to the handbook. A landlord who leaves one out gives the tenant an easy argument that the case is defective.

  • The landlord's name and the tenant's name
  • The reason the tenant is being removed
  • A statement that possession was demanded and refused, plus the three day rent notice where rent is the issue
  • The amount of rent or other money claimed, if any

Attaching the lease or proof of past payments is a common way to show how the amount was reached.

sections.h2: How are the court papers delivered to the tenant?
sections.html:
The summons can be served three ways: by handing it to the tenant, by leaving it with a competent adult who lives in the unit, or by tack and mail. The handbook calls tack and mail the most common method, and it is allowed only when nobody was home when the sheriff tried personal delivery. The postmark date on the envelope should match the day the copy went on the door, and if it does not, the tenant may be able to argue the service was insufficient.

Service method matters for money. When service was by tack and mail and the tenant never answers or appears, the court may still order the tenant to leave but cannot award rent or other damages to the landlord. In most counties the sheriff handles service, though the legal aid flyer notes that in some places a county marshal delivers the warrant.

sections.h2: What are the steps and timing from filing to move-out?
sections.html:
Stages of a Georgia dispossessory case from the DCA Landlord-Tenant Handbook and the Georgia Legal Aid foreclosure flyer
StageWhat happensTiming stated in the source
FilingLandlord swears out the affidavit in the county of the rentalAfter demand is refused
ServiceSheriff or marshal delivers or tacks and mails the summonsDate of service starts the clock
AnswerTenant states defenses and counterclaims, orally or in writingSeven days from service
Rent into courtCourt may order rent paid in if no decision is reachedAfter two weeks without a ruling
HearingHeld when a valid defense is raisedUsually within seven days
Writ of possessionLandlord requests it after a win; sheriff supervises removalTenant moves after seven days

sections.h2: What should a tenant put in the answer?
sections.html:
Every defense and every counterclaim, because Georgia treats anything left out as hard to raise later. A tenant can write the answer or tell it to the clerk, and the handbook adds that an answer on file is treated as an answer until a judge decides otherwise, even when it has no legal defense in it.

Typical defenses in the handbook include a landlord who lost the property to foreclosure and no longer owns it, a rent payment dropped off as the landlord instructed, and a termination that did not follow the lease. Public housing and subsidy tenants may have a right to an informal hearing first. A counterclaim might cover unmade repairs that damaged belongings. The answer must be truthful, since a knowingly false statement in a court filing can be a crime.

sections.h2: Is there any way back after a missed answer?
sections.html:
Rarely, and the handbook says so plainly. A tenant who was served by tack and mail and misses the deadline usually cannot count on more time, even after an emergency such as a hospital stay. A tenant who truly never learned of the papers can ask the court for permission to answer late or file a motion to set aside the judgment, explaining why no answer was filed and why the landlord should not be allowed to evict.

If a judge grants that order, the tenant should hand a copy to the landlord and keep one inside the rental in case the sheriff arrives. Payment of rent can also avoid a judgment, but only through the tender defense inside the seven day window. The handbook adds that even after a dismissal a landlord may file again later, so a won case does not end the dispute for good.

sections.h2: What changes when the rented house is sold or foreclosed?
sections.html:
A foreclosure ends the old landlord and tenant relationship, and the new owner can bring an eviction, though the new owner may instead create a fresh lease. The handbook warns that if a new owner demands or accepts rent while an eviction is under way, that can create a tenancy at will. Georgia Courts describes the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act as letting a tenant stay at least 90 days or through the rest of the lease, whichever is longer, with only 90 days if the buyer will live there.

Georgia Legal Aid adds the borrower's side. After a foreclosure sale the former owner no longer owns the home, and the buyer can file for eviction if the owner stays after a demand. The judge's ruling gives seven days to move, and the buyer may offer cash for keys, which usually means leaving the house empty and broom clean by an agreed date.

sections.h2: How does a sale of a tenant-occupied house work in Georgia?
sections.html:
The seller handles the tenant's deposit and, if a case is open, checks its status with the clerk before the closing. The handbook requires the old owner to pass the security deposit to the buyer or return it to the tenant, and a tenant can sue when neither happens. Ask a Georgia attorney whether the lease binds a buyer, since the handbook does not settle that.

The seller also owes the state transfer tax unless the contract says otherwise. The Georgia Superior Court Clerks' Cooperative Authority says the tax is $1 for the first $1,000 and 10 cents for each additional $100 or fractional part, paid before the deed is recorded. Census figures put Georgia at 4,734,436 housing units in 2025, with 65.7 percent of homes owner occupied in 2020 to 2024.

faqs.q: What is a dispossessory warrant in Georgia?
faqs.a: It is the court paper a landlord files to start an eviction. Georgia Courts says the affidavit, also called the warrant, asks the court to return the property to the landlord and award any unpaid rent. A landlord who does not get one cannot lawfully remove a tenant.

faqs.q: How soon after service must a tenant answer an eviction?
faqs.a: Within seven days of actual service, and the next business day when the seventh day is a Saturday, Sunday or holiday. The answer can be written or spoken to the clerk. A tenant who does not answer risks losing without a hearing.

faqs.q: Can a landlord collect rent when the tenant is served by tack and mail?
faqs.a: Not through a default. If the tenant never answers or appears after tack and mail service, the court can order the tenant out but cannot award rent or other money damages.

faqs.q: Who removes the tenant after the landlord wins?
faqs.a: Generally the sheriff supervises the removal after a writ of possession is issued, and the landlord pays the cost. The handbook says the tenant's belongings go on part of the landlord's land unless the landlord and officer agree on another spot. A tenant can still be removed after a judgment even if the tenant pays.

faqs.q: Does a foreclosure sale end a lease on a Georgia rental?
faqs.a: It ends the old landlord and tenant relationship, so the new owner can seek eviction or start a new arrangement. Georgia Courts says the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act can give a tenant at least 90 days or the rest of the lease. Ask the county magistrate court clerk or legal aid how it applies to a specific case.
